title: Ultra-Processed Foods Raised Cancer Survivors' Death Risk by 60 Per Cent. The Tobacco Playbook That Built the Industry Is Now Public.
excerpt: A 15-year study shows UPFs sharply increase cancer mortality. A separate paper reveals US tobacco companies used cigarette-marketing tactics to push the same products worldwide.
body:
Two studies published within days of each other have done something unusual: they have connected the death toll of ultra-processed foods to the business model that made them ubiquitous. The first quantifies the damage. The second names the architects.

## The Mortality Data

A study published in Cancer Epidemiology, Biomarkers & Prevention — a journal of the American Association for Cancer Research — tracked 24,325 people aged 35 and older, of whom 802 were cancer survivors. Over a follow-up period of nearly 15 years, 281 of those cancer survivors died.

Those in the highest third of ultra-processed food consumption had a 48 per cent higher rate of death from any cause and a 59 per cent higher rate of death from cancer compared with those in the lowest third. The researchers controlled for smoking, body mass index, exercise, and cancer type. The effect was not subtle.

A second, larger study in Frontiers in Nutrition, based on 82,221 participants from the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal and Ovarian Cancer Screening Trial, found similar patterns across a 17-year median follow-up. The highest quarter of UPF consumers had a 10 per cent higher risk of death from any cause, a 20 per cent higher risk of death from nervous system diseases, and a 28 per cent higher risk of death from other causes. One finding offered a sliver of comfort: among heavy UPF eaters, those who maintained an otherwise high-quality diet had significantly lower mortality, suggesting that the harm of processed food can be partially offset — but not eliminated — by what else you eat.

## The Tobacco Playbook

On its own, a mortality study is data. What turns it into a story is the paper published simultaneously in the American Journal of Public Health.

Researchers at the University of Kansas, led by Tera Fazzino, documented how Philip Morris, R.J. Reynolds, and other American tobacco companies — after decades of perfecting the art of making cigarettes addictive and marketing them globally — entered the food industry and applied the exact same playbook to ultra-processed products. The strategies included engineering hyperpalatable flavour profiles (the food equivalent of nicotine titration), targeting children through advertising, fighting regulatory oversight through industry lobbying, and expanding aggressively into developing markets.

The result: at least 70 per cent of the US food supply is now composed of hyperpalatable foods. And the practices pioneered by tobacco-owned food companies were adopted across the global food industry, including by companies that never had any connection to cigarettes.

"The food companies continued operating under profit-maximising models that had already proven successful for other addictive products," Fazzino wrote. "It is likely other food companies observed these strategies and adopted similar approaches."

## What This Means for the Indian Kitchen

South Asian families in America occupy a peculiar position in the UPF landscape. The traditional Indian kitchen — built around whole grains, legumes, fresh vegetables, and freshly ground spices — is one of the lowest-UPF diets in the world. Roti from scratch, dal from dry lentils, sabzi from whatever is in season: these are not ultra-processed foods by any definition.

But the second and third generation are not cooking roti from scratch. A 2024 survey by the Asian American Health Initiative found that Indian American households with children under 18 spend between 35 and 42 per cent of their grocery budget on packaged and ready-to-eat products — a figure that has roughly doubled since 2015. The shift is driven by the same forces that drive it everywhere: convenience, dual-income households, and children who grow up eating what their American peers eat.

The Indian packaged food aisle at any Patel Brothers or India Bazaar tells the story. Frozen parathas, instant upma mix, ready-to-eat dal makhani, packaged chaat snacks — products that look Indian but are manufactured through the same industrial processes that define Western UPFs. They carry the same stabilisers, emulsifiers, and flavour enhancers. They just happen to taste like home.

## The Regulatory Moment

Public opinion is shifting faster than policy. A survey cited by Knowridge Science Report found that more than 80 per cent of Americans now support government testing of food additives before they reach the market. Large majorities support warning labels, restrictions on advertising to children, and legal accountability for food companies whose products cause demonstrable harm.

The comparison to tobacco is not metaphorical. It is historical. The same companies. The same tactics. And, increasingly, the same regulatory trajectory: decades of denial, followed by overwhelming evidence, followed by a public that demands action faster than legislatures can deliver it.

For South Asian families, the practical takeaway is not to abandon convenience. It is to recognise that the dal your grandmother made from scratch and the ready-to-eat dal in the foil pouch are not the same food, regardless of what the label says. The ingredients list is the only honest part of the package. Read it the way you would read the fine print on a contract — because that is exactly what it is.
